title: Secret messages: Caesar's cipher
reflection: Byte cracked a message without the key, trying them all. Why is Caesar's cipher not safe today? How do the messages on your phone stay secret?

steps.goal: Julius Caesar wrote secret messages moving each letter 3 places forward in the alphabet (A becomes D, Z goes round to C). mine.challenge() gives a new secret message every time: decode it and make Byte say it.
steps.not_yet: Not yet: Byte has to say the decoded message.
hints: Look at one letter at a time: for i = 1, #secret do local c = secret:sub(i, i) ... end. Spaces stay spaces.
string.byte(c) is the letter's number (A is 65). (n - 65 - 3) % 26 + 65 moves it back 3 places, round the alphabet; string.char turns it into a letter again.

steps.goal: Now the key changes every time: mine.challenge() gives the secret message and the key (how many places each letter was moved). Decode it and make Byte say it.
steps.not_yet: Not yet: Byte has to say the message, decoded with the key MINE gave.
hints: local secret, key = mine.challenge() gives both.
Make the decoding a function, decode(text, key): with the key instead of 3, it works for every key.

steps.goal: An intercepted message, and no key! You only know it contains the word BYTE. Try all the keys, from 1 to 25, and make Byte say the message with the right one.
steps.not_yet: Not yet: Byte has to find the key and say the decoded message.
hints: for key = 1, 25 do ... end tries them all: decode the message with each one.
plain:find("BYTE") is true when the decoded message contains BYTE: then say it, and break stops the loop.
